headline: Wal-Mart enters Canada with 122 Woolco stores
text: Wal-Mart is buying 122 Woolco stores in Canada from Woolworth, for about 335 million dollars, and will convert them to its own name. Last year it bought 91 Pace warehouse clubs from Kmart. Growth at home is slowing as Wal-Mart reaches most of the country.

headline: The Fed raises rates for the first time in five years
text: On 4 February the Federal Reserve raised its target for the rate banks charge each other from 3 to 3.25 percent, its first increase since 1989. Long-term rates had come a long way down: the 10-year Treasury yield averaged 5.3 percent last October, against 15.3 percent in September 1981. Bond prices fell: the 30-year Treasury yield, 6.17 percent on 12 January, and the 10-year yield, which averaged 5.75 percent in January, are both rising. Inflation is only about 2.5 percent (January).
imageCaption: President Clinton meets Fed chairman Alan Greenspan and advisers in the Oval Office

headline: Two flat years for Coca-Cola shares
text: Coca-Cola's total return to shareholders was about 8% in 1993 after about 6% in 1992, short of its record, the company admits. Its business keeps growing: it is now the fourth-largest US company by market value and the largest consumer goods company, worth about 56 billion dollars at the end of 1993. In 1993 it launched the 'Always Coca-Cola' advertising theme worldwide.

headline: The Power Macintosh
text: Apple has started its Power Macintosh line, built on PowerPC processors developed in an alliance with IBM and Motorola. Parts of the Mac's software were rewritten so that older programs still run.

headline: Tobacco bosses tell Congress nicotine is not addictive
text: On 14 April the chief executives of the seven largest US tobacco companies, including Philip Morris, testified under oath before a House subcommittee chaired by Henry Waxman that they did not believe nicotine is addictive.
imageCaption: The chief executives of the seven largest US tobacco companies are sworn in before the House health subcommittee, Washington, 14 April 1994
imageCredit: Ray Lustig / The Washington Post via Getty Images

headline: Disney president Frank Wells dies in a helicopter crash
text: Frank Wells, Disney's president and Michael Eisner's partner since 1984, died in a helicopter crash on 3 April. Since the two took over, Disney's stock market value has risen from about 2 billion to about 22 billion dollars. Euro Disney, which is losing money, has been negotiating with its banks over its debts since March.
imageCredit: The Walt Disney Company (non-free image on English Wikipedia)

headline: Phantom profits at GE's Kidder, Peabody
text: Kidder, Peabody, owned by General Electric since 1986, said that a bond trader, Joseph Jett, had booked about 350 million dollars of profits that did not exist, through trades that were never completed. It is the largest trading fraud yet known, and a blow to General Electric's venture on Wall Street.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Jett (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Electric (read 2026-10-03, on the 1994 sale to PaineWebber). The exact month of disclosure (April 1994) is not confirmed in the sources read; Jett's 'profits' are dated to the first quarter of 1994.
imageCaption: The GE Building at Rockefeller Center, New York, headquarters of GE's NBC television network

headline: Lehman Brothers is independent again
text: American Express has completed the spin-off of Lehman Brothers, the Wall Street bond trading and investment banking house founded in 1850 that it bought in 1984. Lehman, led since April by Richard Fuld, now trades on its own on the New York Stock Exchange. The firm lost $102 million in 1993.
imageCaption: The World Financial Center in Lower Manhattan, where Lehman Brothers had its headquarters

headline: Nokia, the Finnish phone maker, joins the game
text: Nokia of Finland has a secondary listing on the New York Stock Exchange this year. Founded as a pulp mill and long a maker of rubber goods, cables, tyres and televisions, it has sold or spun off many of those businesses and under chief executive Jorma Ollila, in charge since January 1992, is turning itself into a telecoms company. Its equipment carried the world's first GSM call in 1991, and it sold the first commercial GSM phone, the Nokia 1011, in 1992.

headline: Cisco passes $1 billion in sales
text: Cisco reported on August 18 that sales for the fiscal year to July rose 92% to $1.24 billion and net income 83% to $315 million. Chief executive John Morgridge pointed to alliances with IBM, Microsoft and Alcatel and to the acquisitions of Crescendo and Newport Systems.

headline: Anchorage jury orders Exxon to pay 5 billion for the Valdez spill
text: On 16 September a federal jury in Anchorage ordered Exxon to pay 5 billion dollars in punitive damages to about 10,000 fishermen and other Alaskans harmed by the 1989 spill, on top of about 287 million in compensatory damages. It is reported as the largest punitive award ever levied against a corporation.
imageCaption: The Exxon Valdez being towed after the grounding in Prince William Sound, Alaska, 1989

headline: Mosaic Netscape, a new web browser, appears
text: On 13 October Mosaic Communications, a start-up founded in April by Marc Andreessen and Jim Clark, released a test version of its browser, Mosaic Netscape 0.9, free to download.

headline: Sixth hike of the year as bond losses mount
text: On 15 November the Fed raised its rate target by three quarters of a point to 5.5 percent, its sixth increase this year, and banks raised the prime rate to 8.5 percent. The 30-year Treasury yield reached 8.16 percent on 4 November, up from 6.17 percent in January. Inflation is still under 3 percent, yet a 16-year zero-coupon Treasury has lost about 14 percent of its value this year.
imageCaption: President Clinton and Vice President Gore meet Fed chairman Alan Greenspan and others in the Oval Office

headline: Morita steps down; the Columbia write-off
text: Co-founder Akio Morita, who suffered a cerebral haemorrhage last year, stepped down as chairman on 25 November and was succeeded by Norio Ohga. Sony has also taken a 2.7 billion dollar write-off on its American film studio.
imageCaption: Sony chairman Akio Morita laughs as he shows a Walkman in Tokyo

headline: 1994 in review: the Fed's rate rises bring the bond market's worst year
text: The S&P 500 fell 2% in 1994 to 459.27, while the Dow edged up 2.1%. Starting on 4 February the Federal Reserve raised its key rate from 3 to 5.5 percent by November, and the yield on 30-year Treasury bonds rose from 6.2 to 8.2 percent; bond investors lost about 1.5 trillion dollars worldwide. At year's end Mexico's markets are in crisis.
imageCaption: President Clinton and Vice President Gore meet Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan in the Oval Office, 28 January 1993

headline: Lehman cuts costs after a hard first year
text: Lehman Brothers announced a programme of cost cuts at the end of its first year as an independent firm; it employed about 8,500 people. It has also moved its financial year to end in November.

headline: Siemens sells its first GSM mobile phone
text: This year Siemens launched the S1, its first phone for the new digital GSM networks. Siemens has made mobile phones since the C1 of 1985 and is one of the main suppliers of GSM network equipment in Europe.

headline: The PlayStation goes on sale in Japan
text: Sony released the PlayStation in Japan on 3 December, a week after Sega's Saturn. Launches in North America and Europe are planned for 1995.
imageCaption: The original Sony PlayStation (SCPH-1000) with controller
